How Tides Work

By Alex Rivera

Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea levels caused by the gravitational pull of the moon and the sun, together with the rotation of the Earth. Coastal communities have tracked them for thousands of years, and modern tide tables are accurate to within minutes.

The role of the moon

The moon's gravity pulls the ocean toward it, creating a bulge. Read the full guide to lunar gravity or the reference tables for numbers. A second bulge forms on the opposite side of the planet because of inertia, which is why most coasts see two high tides a day.

Spring and neap tides

  • Spring tides occur at new and full moon, when the sun and moon line up.
  • Neap tides occur at the quarter moons, when their pulls partly cancel.

Local geography matters too. Narrow bays and river mouths can amplify the tidal range dramatically, as in the Bay of Fundy, where the difference between high and low water can exceed fifteen meters. Harbor pilots and fishers plan around these differences every day.
